steps: Read the three slots as start, stop and step — the stop is excluded.
Slice the window 2..8 with a step of two and print it.
Check the result holds 2, 4, 6: every other value inside the window.
Slice with a step.realWorld: Downsampling a sensor series to every second reading is one step slice, not a loop with an index counter.
mistakes: Expecting the stop value 8 to appear; the window is cut first, then stepped.
Reading a[2:8:2] as "two elements, then stop".
revision: start:stop:step — stop excluded, step optional.
The window is chosen first, then every step-th element inside it.

steps: Build a 3×3 matrix so row and column indices are easy to check.
Slice the first two rows and every column from index 1.
Confirm the result is 2×2 — rows and columns are cut independently.
Slice rows and columns.realWorld: Reading a data block from a spreadsheet — the first N records, every column past the ID — is one two-axis slice.
mistakes: Swapping the order and slicing columns first.
Forgetting that a bare slice in one slot keeps that whole axis.
revision: The comma separates axes: rows, then columns.
Each axis slices independently; the output shape is what survives.

steps: Slice a range out of an array and keep it in a second name.
Write into the slice.
Print the source array and see the write arrive there.
A slice is a view.realWorld: Cleaning a column region in place works because the slice is the same memory; that same property silently corrupts a dataset when someone assumed a copy.
mistakes: Treating the slice as an independent array and losing the source later.
Believing the assignment created a new buffer.
revision: Basic slicing returns a view onto the same buffer.
Any write through either name is visible through the other.

steps: Create a short range.
Reverse it with a step of -1.
Print the result and note the source is unchanged.
Reverse a row with a negative step.realWorld: Showing the newest reading first is a reversal at display time, with no sort and no copy.
mistakes: Reversing the source in place when only the display needed it reversed.
Assuming the reversal copied the data.
revision: A negative step walks the axis backwards.
The result is a view with negative strides; the values did not move.

steps: Create an array of four values.
Assign zero into the first two positions.
Print the array to confirm only that window changed.
Slice assignment writes through.realWorld: Zeroing a padded block or a missing-data band before a computation is a slice assignment, not twenty individual writes.
mistakes: Assigning to a copy and expecting the original to change.
Using a mismatched shape on the right-hand side.
revision: A basic slice is a window, so assignment edits the source.
The right-hand side is copied into the selected cells.

steps: Build a 4×4 matrix so both axes have something to skip.
Slice every second row and every second column in one expression.
Print the 2×2 result and map each cell back to its source position.
Step in both dimensions.realWorld: Coarse sampling of an image — every second pixel in both directions — is one two-axis step slice.
mistakes: Writing both steps in one slot and expecting a 2-D result.
Forgetting the second axis defaults to everything when its slot is omitted.
revision: Every axis takes its own step after its own comma.
The result is a strided view, not a copy.

steps: Copy an array with .copy().
Write into the copy.
Print both arrays to prove only one changed.
Copy breaks the view link.realWorld: A helper that mutates its input is safe when it receives a copy; passing a slice instead is how a caller's data gets edited.
mistakes: Calling a[:] and thinking it copied — it is still a view.
Copying in a hot loop and paying for an allocation per iteration.
revision: copy() allocates a new buffer.
shares_memory(a, b) is False after a copy, True after a slice.

steps: Create a three-element array.
Slice it far past the end.
Print the result and note there is no IndexError.
Slices clamp instead of failing.realWorld: A page size taken from user input can exceed the row count; a slice returns what exists instead of crashing the endpoint.
mistakes: Assuming out-of-range slices raise so no validation is needed elsewhere.
Confusing clamping (slices) with the IndexError a single index raises.
revision: Slice bounds are clamped to the axis length.
A single out-of-range index still raises IndexError.

steps: Create a range of ten values.
Slice from 2 to 5.
Count the three values and confirm 5 itself is absent.
The end of a slice is exclusive.realWorld: Splitting a dataset into 80/20 chunks is exactly this off-by-one: the first chunk is 0:n, the second n:len.
mistakes: Writing a[2:5] and expecting four values.
Compensating with a[2:6] somewhere else and drifting by one.
revision: The stop index is never included.
slice(2, 5) and a[2:5] are the same rule in two spellings.

steps: Omit the start to mean "from the beginning".
Omit the stop to mean "to the end".
Print both and compare with the explicit bounds.
Omit a bound to keep it open.realWorld: Skipping a CSV header is a[1:] — the omitted stop is why no length arithmetic is needed.
mistakes: Computing len(a) by hand where an omitted stop would do.
Writing a[0:len(a)] and then changing the array without updating it.
revision: An omitted start is 0; an omitted stop is the axis length.
The idiom survives a change in length; the explicit numbers do not.

steps: Apply a step of two with both bounds omitted.
Print the result and count the elements.
Compare with a[1::2] to see the offset version.
A step of two skips elements.realWorld: Separating even and odd days of a series is arange[::2] and arange[1::2], with no index list to maintain.
mistakes: Expecting the step to change the source array.
Confusing the step slot with a second stop value.
revision: The third slot is the step and it can skip or reverse.
It changes the view, never the source.

steps: Take a 3×3 matrix.
Slice rows from index 1 and columns up to index 2.
Print the 2×2 block and verify it is rectangular.
Slice rows and columns at once.realWorld: Dropping a header row and an ID column before modelling is this one expression.
mistakes: Expecting a ragged result from uneven slices — NumPy always returns a rectangle.
Putting the column slice first.
revision: One slice per axis, separated by a comma.
The output is always rectangular.

steps: Slice a middle range into a second name.
Write into the first cell of that slice.
Print the source and the slice to see both change.
Writing through a slice edits the origin.realWorld: In-place cleaning of a feature block works this way; the same aliasing edits the raw data when the intent was a scratch copy.
mistakes: Assuming the second name owns its data.
Copying only when the bug has already changed the source.
revision: A slice shares the buffer; a copy does not.
Ask for .copy() when the two names must diverge.

steps: Reverse a vector with a step of -1.
Reverse both axes of a 2×2 matrix in one expression.
Print both and confirm the shapes are unchanged.
Reverse with a negative step.realWorld: Rotating a matrix by 180° for display is a double reversal — no values are moved in memory.
mistakes: Reversing only one axis and calling it a rotation.
Expecting the shape to change when only the order did.
revision: A negative step walks that axis backwards.
The shape is preserved; only the strides are negated.

steps: Count the values so the target shape is arithmetically possible.
Reshape to (2, 3) and print the grouping.
Try (4, 2) and read the error that proves the count is enforced.
reshape.realWorld: A flat buffer from a file or an image decoder becomes a model input only after a reshape to (rows, features).
mistakes: Reshaping to a shape whose product differs from size.
Assuming reshape reorders values; it only regroups them.
revision: reshape changes shape, never the data or its order.
The element count must be identical before and after.

steps: Flatten a matrix with ravel.
Transpose the same matrix with .T.
Compare the two shapes: (4,) versus (2, 2).
ravel and transpose.realWorld: Moving a matrix between the flat layout a solver wants and the (rows, columns) layout a report needs is these two calls.
mistakes: Treating ravel's result as an independent copy when it may be a view.
Transposing twice in a chain and cancelling the effect.
revision: ravel flattens, .T swaps axes; both are views when the layout allows.
Neither changes the number of values.

steps: Join two length-2 vectors with concatenate and print the length-4 result.
Stack the same two vectors and print the (2, 2) result.
State the difference: one extends an axis, the other adds one.
concatenate and stack.realWorld: Batching rows of new records is concatenate; turning a list of per-sample vectors into a batch matrix is stack.
mistakes: Using stack in a loop and growing a dimension on every iteration.
Concatenating along the wrong axis and doubling the row count.
revision: concatenate joins along an existing axis.
stack creates a new axis, so the rank grows by one.

steps: Write -1 for the dimension you do not want to compute.
Give the other dimension explicitly.
Print the result's shape to confirm NumPy inferred the rows.
reshape with -1 infers the size.realWorld: Batching a stream whose length changes uses reshape(-1, batch), so the batch size stays fixed and the row count adapts.
mistakes: Using -1 on two axes, which cannot be resolved.
Assuming -1 pads to fit; it never invents values.
revision: Exactly one axis may be -1.
The inferred value is size divided by the known dimensions.

steps: Start with a length-3 vector.
Insert an axis with np.newaxis in the index.
Print the shape and confirm it is (3, 1) rather than (1, 3).
newaxis makes a column.realWorld: Subtracting a per-column mean from every row needs the mean as (1, n); a per-row offset needs it as (m, 1).
mistakes: Putting newaxis in the wrong slot and broadcasting the opposite way.
Using reshape where an axis insert would be clearer.
revision: newaxis inserts a length-1 axis at that position.
The slot decides whether it becomes a row or a column.

steps: Stack two equal-shape arrays.
Print the new shape and note the extra leading axis.
Move the axis with axis=1 and compare.
stack adds a new axis.visual:
stack([zeros(2), ones(2)]).shape → (2, 2)
stack(..., axis=1).shape → (2, 2) with the pairs grouped per column
stack adds a new axis.realWorld: Turning a list of per-sample feature vectors into one batch matrix is stack along axis 0, which is what most estimators expect.
mistakes: Stacking arrays of different shapes and reading the error as a data problem.
Confusing stack with concatenate and off-by-one dimensions.
revision: stack grows the rank by one.
All inputs must share the same shape.

steps: Split a length-4 array into two parts.
Print the returned list and each part's shape.
Try a length that does not divide evenly and read the error.
split cuts an array into pieces.realWorld: Train/test splits and mini-batches both start from split or a sliced equivalent.
mistakes: Assuming split pads the last piece.
Forgetting the return value is a list, not an array.
revision: split returns a list of views.
Unequal pieces need array_split.

steps: Flatten a matrix.
Write into the flattened result.
Print the source to prove it did not change.
flatten always copies.realWorld: A function that sorts or shuffles its input safely receives flatten(), because the caller's array cannot be reached through it.
mistakes: Using flatten inside a loop and paying an allocation per call.
Expecting the copy to raise memory errors only on huge arrays.
revision: flatten allocates unconditionally.
shares_memory(a, a.flatten()) is always False.

steps: Flatten a contiguous matrix with ravel.
Check whether the result still points at the source.
Transpose first, then ravel, and compare the answer.
ravel flattens without copying when it c.visual:
a.ravel().base is a → False (the view's base is the flattened view)
shares_memory(a, a.ravel()) → True
ravel flattens without copying when it c.realWorld: Passing a matrix to a flat C API avoids a copy only when ravel can return a view — which depends on the layout, not the call.
mistakes: Mutating the ravel result assuming it is always a copy.
Assuming base identity rather than shares_memory is the alias test.
revision: ravel copies only when the strides forbid a view.
shares_memory is the reliable question; base identity is not.

steps: Reshape a length-4 vector into a 4×1 column.
Broadcast it against a length-4 row and print the shape.
Reshape as 1×4 and repeat to see the transposed behaviour.
reshape turns a vector into a column.realWorld: A per-row offset must arrive as an (m, 1) column, while a per-column offset must arrive as (1, n) — the shape is the whole difference.
mistakes: Using a 1-D vector and expecting the outer product to appear.
Reshaping to (4, 1) but broadcasting it against rows.
revision: reshape can add a length-1 axis without changing the values.
The axis position decides the broadcast direction.

steps: Stack two length-2 vectors with vstack.
Print the (2, 2) result and identify each original row.
Compare with hstack on the same inputs.
vstack stacks arrays into rows.realWorld: Appending a new record to a table is a vstack of the old rows and the new row, kept as an array rather than a list of lists.
mistakes: Using vstack where hstack was meant and doubling the row count.
Stacking a growing array in a loop instead of collecting and stacking once.
revision: vstack adds a first axis, so inputs become rows.
hstack joins along the existing axis instead.

steps: Build a 2×3 matrix.
Print the shape of .T and confirm it is (3, 2).
Write into the transpose and see the source change.
Transpose swaps the axes.visual:
a (2, 3)
a.T (3, 2)
values unmoved — strides reordered
Transpose swaps the axes.realWorld: Most linear algebra expects features as columns or as rows depending on the library; .T supplies the orientation with no copy.
mistakes: Believing .T copied the data.
Forgetting that a write through the transpose reaches the original.
revision: .T reverses the axis order and returns a view.
Size is unchanged; only the shape and strides swap.

steps: Reshape a flat range into a matrix.
Write into the first cell of the matrix.
Print the flat source and confirm the value arrived.
reshape returns a view when it can.realWorld: Filling a matrix in place without doubling memory depends on reshape returning a view, which is why the layout matters.
mistakes: Assuming reshape copied and mutating freely.
Relying on a view where a non-contiguous source forces a copy.
revision: reshape copies only when the strides cannot express the new shape.
Use .copy() when independence is required.

steps: Stack two vectors as rows with vstack.
Join the same vectors end to end with hstack.
Stack them into a new axis and compare all three shapes.
Stack and concatenate.realWorld: Feature blocks are joined with hstack, record batches with vstack, and per-sample vectors become a batch with stack.
mistakes: Mixing the three and getting a silently wrong axis.
Concatenating arrays whose non-joined axes disagree.
revision: vstack adds rows, hstack adds columns.
stack creates a new axis; concatenate uses an existing one.
